title: How to Age With Grace
excerpt: Our culture handles aging by hiding it or fighting it with ever more elaborate programs of postponement. Christians can simply look at it, grieving what it takes without grieving as those who have no hope.
body:
Our whole culture is organized around the refusal to age. We hide the old in facilities and the dying in hospitals, and for those still in the game we sell an endless war against the clock, the creams and procedures and supplements that promise to hold off what is coming. The message underneath all of it is that aging is a defeat, a failure of will or money or vigilance, something to be fought to the last and never accepted. This is a strange way to treat the one thing that happens to everyone who is fortunate enough to live.

Christians can do something the culture cannot. We can simply look at aging, without the panic and without the denial. We can grieve what it takes, honestly, and still refuse the terror, because the body's story does not end at the grave. Aging with grace is not pretending it does not hurt. It is facing it with hope.

## Honor your own decline

There is real loss in aging and it does no good to pretend otherwise. The strength fades. The body that once did what you asked now negotiates. The names come slower, the stairs come harder, the mirror shows someone you do not quite recognize. Faith does not require you to be cheerful about this. The Psalms include the prayer, do not cast me off in the time of old age, do not forsake me when my strength is spent. That is an honest prayer, and God put it in the book.

So grieve what is real. Aging takes things, and the losses deserve to be named, not minimized with a forced smile. But grieve as one who has hope, because the grief is not the whole story. The decline of the body is not the decline of the person. The outer self wastes away, Paul writes, while the inner self is being renewed day by day. The two can run in opposite directions at once, the body weakening while the soul deepens, and that is not denial. That is the actual design.

## There is a glory reserved for the old

Our culture worships youth, and the church has too often gone along, building everything around the young and quietly sidelining the old. Scripture flips it. Gray hair is a crown of glory, Proverbs says, gained in a righteous life. The old were meant to be the keepers of wisdom and memory, the ones who had walked the long road and could tell you what they found.

If you are aging, you have something the young cannot have and cannot fake, the perspective that only decades give. The faithfulness of God across a whole life, seen from the far end. The lessons paid for in failure and grief. This is not consolation for losing your youth. It is a real glory the young do not yet possess. The task of the old is not to mimic the young but to become what only age can make, a person of seasoned wisdom whose presence steadies a room. Do not despise your gray hair. It is a crown.

## Receive help as you once gave it

The hardest turn in aging, for the strong especially, is the move from giver to receiver. There comes a point where you need help with things you once did without thinking, and for a lifelong helper this can feel like a humiliation. It is not. It is a return to the truth you always lived inside but could ignore while you were strong, that you are a dependent creature, held by God and meant to be held by others.

Jesus told Peter that when he was old he would stretch out his hands and another would dress him and carry him where he did not want to go. Even that loss of independence, Jesus framed as a way of glorifying God. To receive care with grace, to let others do for you what you can no longer do for yourself, is not the end of usefulness. It is its own kind of witness, a daily lesson in dependence that the proud and able never get to learn.

## And get the care your body needs

A plain word among the theology. Aging well includes ordinary good medical care, and there is nothing unfaithful about it. Get the screenings, treat the conditions, take the medications that keep you well and present. Pay attention to the body and mind both, because the changes of age, in memory and mood as much as in the joints, often have real help available. Stewardship does not stop because you are old. Caring for an aging body is still caring for a gift.

## The hope that changes everything

The reason a Christian can age without terror is the resurrection. This body will weaken and fail and be buried, and that is not the end of it. We grieve, but not as those without hope, because the same God who made this body intends to raise it, renewed and incorruptible. The old believer is not winding down toward nothing. He is, strange as it sounds, closer to the beginning than the young are, nearer to the morning when the body is raised. That hope does not erase the losses. It puts them in their place.

## This week

If you are aging, do two things. Name one loss honestly, to God or to someone you trust, without rushing to make it okay, because the grief is allowed. And name one thing the years have given you, some wisdom or perspective or steadiness that the young around you do not yet have, and find one young person to give it to this week, a word, a story, an hour of real attention. You are not winding down toward nothing. You are a crown of glory carrying a lifetime of God's faithfulness, headed for a morning when this tired body is raised.
